soil-found-060.title: Hydrolysis and carbonation, the acid attack on rock
soil-found-060.text: Weathering rock helps set how much carbon dioxide stays in the air. Silicate weathering consumes carbonic acid and leaves alkaline bicarbonate solutions, an important control on atmospheric carbon dioxide and climate. The reactions behind it are {{ref:soil-form-172}} and carbonation. In them, only part of a mineral dissolves, and the rest becomes a new solid, often one of the fine minerals of clay. Most of it is driven by acid: protons in acidic water attack the chemical bonds in mineral crystals. Carbonic acid, from dissolved carbon dioxide, is the main source of those protons, though organic acids also matter. The textbook case is the potassium mineral of {{ref:soil-form-143}}, one of the group in {{ref:soil-form-141}}. With carbonic acid and water, it yields {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, silicic acid, and potassium and bicarbonate ions in solution. The weakest bonds between metal and oxygen go first. So igneous minerals weather in roughly the order they formed, a sequence described in {{ref:soil-chem-186}}. There are exceptions, such as silica, which is unusually unstable. Carbonation is the form driven by dissolved carbon dioxide. It can also turn minerals inherited from rock ({{ref:soil-form-140}}) into the {{ref:soil-chem-235}} of {{ref:soil-found-034}}, as when forsterite weathers to magnesite.

soil-chem-238.title: How layered silicate minerals differ in charge and surface area
soil-chem-238.text: Layered silicate minerals of one family can differ enormously in how much they hold. Phyllosilicates differ mainly in cation exchange capacity, CEC, and in reactive surface area, which depend on {{ref:soil-chem-085}} and on whether the interlayer admits cations. {{ref:soil-chem-088}} has little substitution and does not expand, so its CEC is 2-16 cmol(+) per kg and its surface is only external, 5-15 m2 per g. {{ref:soil-chem-094}} and chlorite have substantial substitution, but a tightly bound K+ or hydroxide interlayer blocks expansion, so CEC is limited: 20-40 for the first and 10-40 for chlorite. {{ref:soil-chem-091}} admits interlayer cations, giving CEC 60-120 and an internal surface of 570-660 m2 per g, and soils rich in it swell and shrink strongly. {{ref:soil-chem-095}} has CEC of 100-150 but expands little, because its charge, concentrated near the interlayer, binds cations tightly and restricts water entry. Fe/Al oxyhydroxides have CEC near 0-3 but 200-500 m2 per g of surface, and amorphous minerals of aluminum and silicon range from 5 to 350 CEC.

soil-chem-235.title: Secondary minerals: what weathering builds from the wreckage
soil-chem-235.text: Weathering makes new minerals as well as breaking down old ones. A secondary mineral is a by-product of chemical weathering, formed by partial alteration of a primary mineral ({{ref:soil-form-140}}) or by precipitation from components dissolved from other minerals. Primary minerals form as the original molten crust cools and solidifies, while secondary minerals form from their breakdown products. In heavily weathered soils secondary minerals dominate, including iron and aluminum oxides from primary igneous silicates. Most are hydrated minerals of aluminum and silicon (phyllosilicates, or the layered silicate minerals) or Fe and Al oxyhydroxides, which are stable in soils. Phyllosilicates are the most chemically reactive inorganic phases in soil; their amount and type influence porosity, swelling, compressibility, {{ref:soil-chem-068}} and exchange capacity, and hydraulic conductivity. In glaciated Canada most secondary minerals formed before the last glaciation and were redeposited, so little has formed since compared with the amount inherited.

soil-chem-004.title: Rocks that leave acid soils behind
soil-chem-004.text: Some soils are acid from the start because of the rock beneath them. Acidic parent materials are rocks and sediments whose weathering acidifies the soils formed on them. Granites and allied igneous rocks are called 'acidic' because their abundant free quartz yields silicic acid on weathering. They are also low in calcium and magnesium. Sulfide-rich shale and coal, when hydrated and oxidized, produce sulfuric acid, much stronger than silicic acid. Many coal soils are too acidic for vigorous plant growth. Clays laid down in the sea are often sulfide-rich and become very acidic if drained to an oxidizing state.

soil-bio-154.title: Rhizobacteria, the bacteria that live on roots
soil-bio-154.text: Not every bacterium on a root is a friend. Rhizobacteria are bacteria that live with plant roots and can harm plant growth, leave it alone or help it. In practice the word usually means the helpful ones, described in {{ref:soil-bio-155}}; they make up about 2–5% of rhizosphere bacteria. Some colonize the root surface or the spaces between outer root cells, often forming nodules. Others live inside the plant, in the apoplast, the spaces outside its cells, the subject of {{ref:soil-bio-202}}. One of their most useful acts is turning N2 gas, which plants cannot use, into ammonia the host can take up. That service is costly. Building and keeping nodules can take 12–25% of a plant's total photosynthetic output. Rhizobacteria also release organic acids and phosphate-splitting enzymes that turn insoluble soil phosphorus into usable forms such as H2PO4−. Free-living nitrogen fixers live just outside the roots of many grasses. In rice they supply more fixed nitrogen when the plant's demand is high. Organic amendments such as sugarcane straw, goat manure and filter mud boost these free-living helpers, even without nodules.

soil-class-021.title: The FAO map legend that became a world system
soil-class-021.text: The first truly international soil classification began life as the key to a map. The FAO soil classification, developed by the {{ref:soil-env-372}}, is a supra-national system that generalizes how soils form from the interaction of the main soil-forming factors. It started as the legend of the FAO–UNESCO map of the world's soils, published from 1971 to 1981 in 10 volumes at a scale of 1:5 million. Rudi Dudal led the 1974 legend. It gathered ideas from national systems, among them the diagnostic horizons of the USDA's 1960 '7th approximation'. Its 106 soil units were mapped as associations named for the dominant unit, with phases marking local land features, three texture classes and three slope classes. Simple and broad, it fitted most soils from field descriptions alone. It was meant for continental maps, not local ones. The 1988 Revised Legend had 153 soil units in 28 major soil groupings, and it still underlies the Harmonized World Soil Database. United Nations projects applied the system, and many countries adapted it. Many of its names are known widely, with similar meanings. In the 1974 legend, thin soils on calcareous rock were called {{ref:soil-class-050}} and those on acid rock were called {{ref:soil-class-040}}. The WRB replaced it in 1998.

soil-form-162.title: Soils of British Columbia and Yukon
soil-form-162.text: No other part of Canada has soils as varied as British Columbia and Yukon, thanks to a varied geologic history, rugged terrain and a wide climate range. The region holds all ten soil orders of the Canadian system. {{ref:soil-class-138}} soils have the largest extent in British Columbia, on {{ref:soil-chem-004}} under cool, humid conditions, and {{ref:soil-class-133}} soils are the other dominant order, on loamy glacial tills in the Interior plateaus and boreal forest. Cryosols occur in permafrost areas of northern Yukon and on high mountain peaks, while {{ref:soil-class-123}} soils occur only in the arid Central Interior. {{ref:soil-class-139}} soils mark landslide-prone and avalanche-prone slopes and the Fraser Delta, and drained {{ref:soil-class-127}} soils in the Fraser Valley are among the province's most productive farm soils. Mining leaves {{ref:soil-class-044}}; in metal mining the chief concern is acid rock drainage, because sulphide minerals such as {{ref:soil-chem-134}} weather rapidly to sulfuric acid.

soil-form-167.title: Soils of Quebec
soil-form-167.text: Quebec's soils sit in bands from south to north, and there are seven soil orders in them. They formed over the last 6,000 to 10,000 years, after the Laurentide Ice Sheet retreated, on parent materials that follow the Canadian Shield, the Appalachians and the sedimentary St. Lawrence valley. {{ref:soil-class-138}} soils cover 39% of Quebec, Brunisols 17% and Organic soils 8%. Dystric Brunisols can turn into them over several thousand years, as on the North Shore. After glaciation the Champlain Sea left salt-rich clay in the St. Lawrence Lowlands; leaching of the salt and river incision made it unstable, causing over 700 landslides and {{ref:soil-water-101}}. Only a small area has high agricultural potential: Canada Land Inventory Classes 1 to 3 total about 0.28 ha per Quebecer, the smallest of any province, and about 80% of them are cropland, so conserving them matters.

soil-form-169.title: Soils of the Atlantic Provinces
soil-form-169.text: Seven of Canada's ten soil orders occur in Atlantic Canada, but heavy precipitation and coarse, acidic glacial till make {{ref:soil-class-138}} soils dominant. The soils are often stony or shallow to bedrock, so the four provinces hold only about 1.5% of Canada's farmland, and only Prince Edward Island has more farmland than forest. Four ecozones divide the region. The Atlantic Maritime is warmest, about 7 degrees C with 1250 mm of rain a year, on mostly sedimentary Paleozoic rock. The Taiga Shield and Arctic Cordillera are colder, on Precambrian gneiss and granite with thin till and exposed rock. The Canada Land Inventory finds no Class 1 land here; Class 2 is about 588,000 ha, Class 3 about 2,275,000 ha and Class 4 about 2,507,000 ha, and most of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland is Class 7.

soil-form-163.title: Soils of the Prairie Provinces
soil-form-163.text: In southern Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, over 80% of the land is agricultural, the most heavily converted in Canada, and the kind of farming follows soil capability. True prairie covers only the southern part. About one-third of the region sits on Canadian Shield rock and two-thirds on sedimentary rock; igneous rock yields acidic sandy, gravelly parent materials, sedimentary rock neutral to alkaline loamy ones. {{ref:soil-class-123}} soils dominate the southern grassland, {{ref:soil-class-133}} soils the northern mixed forest, Brunisols the acidic Shield and Organic Cryosols the cold, saturated peats near Hudson Bay. The pattern is set by bedrock and by the rain shadow of the Western Cordillera. Crops once centred on spring wheat with summerfallow; today canola, pulses and flax are grown, with continuous cultivation and {{ref:soil-agri-099}} or no-till. Under the Canada Land Inventory, classes 1 to 4 sustain field crops and classes 5 and 6 suit only forage.

soil-form-165.title: From grassland to forest: the Parkland transition
soil-form-165.text: Walk north from the grassland and the soil changes as tree litter replaces grass as the main organic input. In the transitional Parkland the Ah horizon lightens and begins to bleach, forming an Ahe horizon; these are Dark Gray {{ref:soil-class-123}} soils. Further north, in continuous Mixedwood forest, an LFH litter layer sits on the mineral soil over a bleached Ae horizon and a clay-richer Bt horizon, underlain by a carbonate-bearing C horizon. These are Gray {{ref:soil-class-133}} soils, which also form on glacio-lacustrine deposits in north-central Manitoba.

soil-phys-007.title: Crumbs within crumbs: the aggregate hierarchy
soil-phys-007.text: A soil crumb is usually built of smaller crumbs, which are built of smaller ones still. The aggregate hierarchy is the idea that aggregates form in levels, larger and looser ones made from smaller, denser ones. Particles join into microaggregates below 250 μm, and these into macroaggregates above 250 μm. Fungal hyphae and roots, the temporary binders, hold macroaggregates together. Transient long-chain sugars and persistent compounds hold microaggregates. Yet organic matter's role is hard to pin down, and in some soils it is not the main binder.

soil-phys-043.title: Specific surface area: why tiny grains do the most work
soil-phys-043.text: Surface is where soil does its chemistry. Specific surface area is the surface area of soil particles relative to their amount, defined as area per unit mass. Surface area per unit weight rises as average particle size falls, so sand has the least and is least active, silt is intermediate and clay is the most active. The mineral crystals in clay form thin plates and typically have 10 to 1,000 square metres of surface per gram. In one table, very coarse sand (2.00-1.00 mm) has 90 particles per gram and 11 cm2/g, fine sand (0.25-0.10 mm) 46,000 and 91 cm2/g, and silt 5,776,000 and 454 cm2/g. That large surface, with many negative charges, gives clay its high capacity to retain water and nutrients, and the water held after free drainage ({{ref:soil-water-177}}) depends on it. Particles of one textural class share properties tied to surface area, such as moisture retention, but not those tied to composition, such as the ability to hold nutrient cations ({{ref:soil-chem-047}}). One source instead describes it as the surface-area-to-volume ratio of particles.

soil-agri-121.title: Minimum tillage: only as much as the crop needs
soil-agri-121.text: Minimum tillage avoids primary tillage entirely. This system for conserving soil keeps manipulation to the minimum a crop needs, without turning the soil over. Secondary tillage is practiced only to a small extent. The system also includes minimum furrowing, organic fertilizer, {{ref:soil-agri-217}} and minimal use of chemicals. Some minimum or low-till methods mix tilled and untilled approaches, for example shallow disc harrowing without ploughing, or {{ref:soil-agri-120}}.

soil-agri-170.title: Web Soil Survey: soil maps on demand
soil-agri-170.text: New surveys of the same county once took 30 to 60 years to appear. Web Soil Survey, run by the USDA's {{ref:soil-hist-050}}, ended that wait. US surveys are no longer printed as books. They are published online, holding everything in the old county reports plus extra tools, and can be updated as needed. It gives access to data from the {{ref:soil-hist-051}}, building on the {{ref:soil-agri-082}} and the {{ref:soil-agri-084}}. A user picks an area of interest anywhere in the United States where survey data exist. The Soil Map tab then shows the component soil map units, and a report can be saved as a PDF. The Soil Data Explorer gives properties for each map unit, such as depth to water table, surface texture, bulk density, pH and depth to a restrictive layer. It also gives suitability ratings, with reasons, for uses such as dwellings with basements, local roads and streets, vegetative productivity and wastewater disposal by irrigation. It is one recognized basis, alongside measured infiltration rates, for choosing the hydrologic soil group of a site.

soil-agri-180.title: Choosing a cover crop for the job
soil-agri-180.text: Different cover crops are grown for different primary purposes. Grasses such as cereal rye and oats catch and cycle nutrients. Legumes such as hairy vetch and red clover fix nitrogen with Rhizobium as green manures (see {{ref:soil-fert-026}}). Fast-growing competitive species such as buckwheat and sorghum-sudangrass smother weeds. Brassicas such as mustards and radishes biofumigate pests with glucosinolates and isothiocyanates. Strong-rooted crops such as cereal rye, radishes, hairy vetch and alfalfa loosen compacted soil, while sorghum-sudangrass, cereal rye and sunn hemp build biomass and organic matter. Ecologists separate canopy functions (aboveground biomass) from root functions (belowground biomass), and choice can follow the traits wanted. Cover-crop grasses are more likely than legumes to increase {{ref:soil-found-045}}, and some grow as much or more biomass underground as above. Hairy vetch or crimson clover may yield 1.5 to over 4 tons dry weight per acre, mature cereal rye 3-5 tons, and early-terminated crops as little as half a ton. The gains are measurable. A five-year California clover experiment raised organic matter in the top 2 inches from 1.3% to 2.6%. Pooled experiments found cover crops raised organic matter 8.5% over original levels and soil nitrogen 12.8%.

soil-bio-008.title: Five hundred sheep beneath a football pitch
soil-bio-008.text: The organisms living beneath a football pitch are estimated to equal the size of 500 sheep. Soil biodiversity is the relationship between soil and that variety of life, including the aspects of soil that can be managed with it in mind. Soil is chiefly a habitat for microbes such as bacteria and fungi. It also houses tiny animals such as {{ref:soil-bio-274}} and {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, small ones such as potworms and {{ref:soil-bio-209}}, and larger ones such as earthworms, termites and millipedes. Their primary role is to recycle dead organic material from the plant-based food web above ground. In turn, their activity is a primary factor in how soil forms, physically and chemically. The link shows on maps: natural and farm vegetation boundaries closely follow soil boundaries, even at continental and global scales. Microbial exudates are now accepted as the main force that binds soil particles into clumps and shields carbon from further breakdown. Soil health depends on this diversity. Living covers on the soil and carbon-containing amendments improve it. {{ref:soil-agri-004}}, {{ref:soil-agri-192}}, legume intercrops and organic inputs all correlate with more diverse soil life.

soil-bio-104.title: Mor, where litter piles up and fungi rule
soil-bio-104.text: Mor and thick moder were long confused under one name, raw humus. Mor is the humus form of coniferous forests and open shrublands in which litter decomposes very slowly and piles up on the soil, barely mixing into the mineral soil. Evergreen needles, shrub twigs and woody debris rot slowly because of low pH, few nutrients, much lignin, tannin or terpenes, and cool, wet conditions. Bacteria are inactive at low pH and earthworms are absent, so fungi do most of the work. A thick OL horizon lies on an OF horizon matted with roots and fungal hyphae, then a variable OH horizon. The change to mineral soil is sharp, with no A horizon. Organic matter instead leaches in solution through the E horizon to the B horizon, as in podzolization. High C:N and C:P ratios lock up nitrogen and starve plants, which then drop nutrient-poor litter, closing a loop. Ectomycorrhizal and ericoid fungi pass nitrogen straight from the slowly rotting remains to plants. Mor goes with very cold climates, high altitude or latitude, pines and shrublands, or heavy pollution.

soil-bio-276.title: Humus: the dark, stable core of soil organic matter
soil-bio-276.text: Humus is light for its bulk. Its bulk density is just 0.05 to 0.25 g per cubic centimetre, and its cation exchange capacity tops 200 cmol(+) per kilogram. It is the stable, dark, amorphous fraction of soil organic matter left after most added residues have decomposed, bound to clays and oxides that shield it from microbes. It has high porosity and water holding capacity. Its approximate composition is 50% carbon, 35% oxygen, 8% hydrogen, 5% nitrogen and 2% sulfur. It commonly supplies 20 to 30% or more of a soil's cation exchange capacity, buffers pH and binds peds into aggregates. Arable soils average 2 to 3% humus, from under 1% to over 12%. Keeping it takes work. Cultivated soils lose humus by decomposition at 1 to 2% per year. Holding the normal level needs 1000 to 5000 kg per hectare of organic material a year, since added material does not permanently raise it. Rotations with grasses and legumes, {{ref:soil-agri-099}} and residue management help sustain it.

soil-bio-283.title: Sporosarcina pasteurii, the bacterium that turns sand to stone
soil-bio-283.text: Give one soil bacterium calcium and {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, and loose sand sets solid. Sporosarcina pasteurii is a gram-positive, rod-shaped bacterium, 0.5 to 1.2 micrometres wide and 1.3 to 4.0 micrometres long. It forms endospores and thrives at pH 9 to 10, surviving up to pH 11.2. It secretes the enzyme {{ref:soil-fert-224}} to hydrolyse it, which feeds the bacterium nitrogen, carbon and energy. The carbonate ions released react with calcium to precipitate {{ref:soil-found-118}} that cements sand grains. This is {{ref:soil-bio-067}}. The organism is non-pathogenic and makes a great deal of this enzyme, so it is a common choice for the job. It is proposed for self-healing concrete and other bio-cement uses.

soil-bio-285.title: How organic matter feeds plants
soil-bio-285.text: Plants need 17 elements. Carbon and oxygen come from air and the rest mainly from soil, with availability affected directly or indirectly by organic matter, the heart of {{ref:soil-fert-149}}. Decomposition converts nutrients to plant-usable forms, produces cation exchange capacity that retains calcium, potassium, magnesium and ammonium, and makes organic molecules that hold micronutrients such as zinc and iron. Siderophores make micronutrients more available, so roots grow longer and more branched. Humic substances may stimulate roots by raising micronutrient availability and changing gene expression. In one experiment humic acids in nutrient solution increased tomato and corn growth and root branching. Soil organisms fix nitrogen and dissolve phosphorus, and with too little food they are scarce and more fertilizer is needed. Physical effects matter as well. Organic matter improves structure, raising infiltration, water-holding capacity and root growth into permeable soil. Good tilth stores more water between rains and reduces erosion. Poor tilth means broken aggregates, compaction, and less aeration and water storage, and a layer can become too compact for roots. Topsoil's good qualities arise because it is rich in organic matter and life, not because of its position. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}, {{ref:soil-bio-089}} and {{ref:soil-found-014}}.

soil-bio-286.title: Organic matter and the nitrogen cycle
soil-bio-286.text: Each percent of organic matter in the top 6 inches holds about 1,000 pounds of nitrogen. Almost all soil nitrogen is part of organic matter, in forms plants cannot use directly. Plants take up most of theirs as nitrate and a little as ammonium, and small amounts of amino acids and small proteins can also be absorbed. Each year bacteria and fungi convert some organic nitrogen to ammonium and other bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate. A crop may draw 20-50% of its nitrogen from mineralized organic matter. Other sources are manure, nitrogen-fixing bacteria (large amounts under legumes), rain and snow deposition, and industrially fixed fertilizer, the largest addition for most grain crops. Losses follow. Nitrate leaches readily, especially from sandy and tile-drained soils, reaching groundwater or causing dead zones. Uncomposted manure or surface fertilizer may lose up to 30% by volatilization. {{ref:soil-fert-108}} by bacteria in saturated soils turns nitrate into N2 and nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas estimated as agriculture's largest greenhouse contribution that also thins the ozone layer. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-314.title: Forests, farmland and soil carbon
soil-bio-314.text: Cutting down a forest typically lowers its {{ref:soil-env-106}}, and planting trees again may partly restore the original levels. The rate varies. Boreal reforestation gains carbon more slowly than other climates because trees grow slowly, and the previous land use and the type of disturbance control the rate. Afforested farmland gains more carbon in the soil than pasture or grassland, and mine-disturbed soils also gain a lot. Where they suit the site, deciduous trees raise it faster than conifers. Over time they also store more of it in the mineral soil than in the forest floor.

soil-bio-319.title: Converting organic matter to carbon, and its weakness
soil-bio-319.text: {{ref:soil-env-108}} and soil organic matter are different quantities. They are routinely converted by assuming that carbon is 58% of organic matter mass, a factor of 1.72. That figure comes from Waksman and Stevens (1930), who urged caution. Organic matter also holds hydrogen (about 4%) and oxygen (about 30%), and these vary with the state of decomposition. Reviews of many studies find that actual factors are usually higher than 1.72, meaning carbon is a smaller share of organic matter. The best approach is separate direct analyses. Otherwise, state what was analyzed and how values were converted.

soil-chem-005.title: How fertilizers make soil more acidic
soil-chem-005.text: Feeding a crop can sour the soil beneath it. Fertilizer-induced acidification is the lowering of soil pH by chemical fertilizers, above all ammonium-based nitrogen and sulfur fertilizers. It is one cause behind {{ref:soil-chem-001}}. Most nitrogen fertilizers acidify, ammonium-based ones most of all: ammonium sulfate, diammonium and monoammonium phosphate, and {{ref:soil-fert-071}}. {{ref:soil-fert-021}} and compost acidify less. {{ref:soil-fert-112}} of ammonium releases hydrogen ions and nitric acid as byproducts, which keep acidifying the soil. Nitrate sources with little or no ammonium, such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium nitrate, do not acidify and can slightly raise pH. Elemental sulfur and iron sulfate can be highly acidifying, while potassium sulfate has no significant effect on pH. Most commercial nitrogen fertilizers are acid forming, but many manures are not. Generally 4-7 pounds of lime neutralize the acid from each pound of nitrogen applied. Monoculture with chemical fertilization often brings acidification and degradation. Sugarcane monoculture raised acidity, lowered fertility and shifted soil microbes.

soil-chem-222.title: Saline, sodic and saline-sodic: three ways soil goes salty
soil-chem-222.text: Two soils can look equally ruined and need opposite cures. Salt-affected soils are classed as saline, sodic or saline-sodic by total salt (EC) and sodium content (SAR, ESP). Saline soils have EC above 4 dS/m but SAR below 13 and ESP below 15%, with pH usually under 8.5 and flocculated colloids. {{ref:soil-chem-009}} soils have EC below 4 dS/m but SAR above 13 and ESP above 15%, and pH usually above 8.5 from hydrolysis of Na2CO3. Saline-sodic soils have EC above 4 dS/m, SAR above 13 and ESP above 15%. Their pH is usually below 8.5 and they stay flocculated. Sodium explains the difference. Hydrated Na+ between clay particles cancels the binding electrostatic forces, and extra water layers push the particles apart. That disperses the soil, and high pH also disperses organic matter. Saline soils stay aggregated with high infiltration, so they leach easily. Dispersed sodic and saline-sodic soils infiltrate poorly and usually need gypsum. Calcium replacing monovalent Na+ promotes aggregation and infiltration, and the displaced sodium and salts are leached. Saline drainage may be diverted through subsurface drains. Salt-tolerant crops such as barley or sunflower, and trees, can take up salts, but prevention is better than reclamation. Natural sources include mineral weathering, atmospheric deposition, seawater intrusion, saline groundwater and natural brines. Human sources include salty irrigation water, salty fertilizers, manure, {{ref:soil-fert-045}}, compost and road salt.

soil-chem-239.title: Why Canadian clays came from the ice
soil-chem-239.text: Most of the layered silicate minerals in Canadian soils did not form where they now sit. The continental glaciers delivered them in the parent material. {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, {{ref:soil-chem-135}} and chlorite come straight from the Canadian Shield, while others in the Interior Plains derive from degraded Cretaceous sediments. Interior Plains clay is mostly {{ref:soil-chem-091}}, that same mineral, chlorite and some kaolin. The older Devonian and Silurian sediments of the St. Lawrence Lowlands give that mineral, chlorite, {{ref:soil-chem-095}} and kaolin. Little alteration shows across regions. The exceptions are Podzolic and some Brunisolic and Gleysolic soils, where inherited chlorite weathers to expandable {{ref:soil-found-033}}.

soil-chem-242.title: Pyrite, sulfuric acid and gypsum in soil
soil-chem-242.text: {{ref:soil-chem-134}} and other sulfide minerals are absent from well-drained soils. They may occur in poorly drained Gleysolic or Organic soils, tidal soils and mine wastes. Exposed to air, it oxidizes to iron and sulfuric acid: 2FeS2 + 7O2 + 2H2O gives 2Fe2+ + 4H+ + 4SO4 2-. Oxidation of sulfides can push soil pH below 2.0. Mining or excavation that exposes sulfides is mainly responsible for acid rock drainage. Sulfate from sulfide oxidation or other sources forms gypsum, usually at high pH with soluble calcium present.

soil-class-006.title: USDA soil taxonomy: six levels from order to series
soil-class-006.text: The United States sorts its soils into 12 orders, 47 suborders, about 185 great groups, about 1,000 subgroups, about 4,500 families and more than 14,000 series. USDA soil taxonomy is the classification of the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the {{ref:soil-hist-051}}. It sorts soils by their properties into six levels, from most general to most specific: order, suborder, great group, subgroup, family and series. The lab manual describes it as a quantitative hierarchy running from 12 broad orders to more than 23,000 series, and says it helps carry management research between similar soils worldwide. Sources differ on the series count: the more than 14,000 above is the United States figure. It uses properties that can be measured: depth, moisture, temperature, texture, structure, cation exchange capacity, base saturation, clay mineralogy, organic matter and salt content. It is a hierarchical hybrid of natural and objective criteria, designed to guide land use and {{ref:soil-agri-063}}, and it supplies the core criteria for U.S. soil map units. Order names end in -sol, and the criteria for orders reflect major differences in how soils formed. It builds on {{ref:soil-class-001}}, {{ref:soil-class-005}}, {{ref:soil-found-001}} and {{ref:soil-form-017}}. Guy Donald Smith, director of USDA soil survey investigations, originally developed it as a substantial revision of the strictly natural 1938 system. Work began by 1945. A series of approximations followed, the 7th in 1960, and the taxonomy appeared in 1975 with 10 orders and in 1999, revised, with 12.

soil-env-352.title: Laboratory tests that measure how alive a soil is
soil-env-352.text: For years the standard soil test was chemical, and that gave a chemical bias that favored quick-fix fertilizer use. Laboratory soil health tests add biological and physical indicators to the chemical ones, to assess the soil processes that support ecosystem services. As of 2020 no single standard soil health test exists, though all agree it needs biological, physical and chemical indicators and interpretation by climate and texture. This is the quantitative end of {{ref:soil-env-177}}. Aggregate stability reflects infiltration, crusting and tilth and responds fast to reduced tillage, cover crops or manure. Available water capacity depends more on texture than on management. Soil organic matter is often the single most important indicator but changes too slowly. {{ref:soil-env-286}}, oxidized by potassium permanganate, responds quickly, and soil protein does too, especially with more legumes. Soil respiration integrates microbial abundance and activity and tracks nitrogen mineralization potential. The bean root rot bioassay gauges root health and disease pressure from nematodes and fungi such as Fusarium, Pythium and Rhizoctonia. Context adds tests. Salts and sodium should be tested in arid regions and greenhouses, and heavy metals, radioactive materials, solvents and petroleum products in urban or industrial soils.

soil-fert-034.title: Using finished compost on fields and in beds
soil-fert-034.text: A field needs only a thin dusting of compost, about 6 mm (0.24 in). Compost applied is finished compost used on fields, in beds and in growing mixes to add organic matter and nutrients (see {{ref:soil-fert-028}}). On open fields it is broadcast in that thin layer and worked in before planting. A layer of 25 mm (0.98 in) or more is used to rebuild poor soils or control erosion. Added to soil, {{ref:soil-agri-139}} or peat, it improves tilth and supplies humus and nutrients. Tilled in, it raises organic matter and overall fertility. Compost is rarely used alone. It is mixed with sand, grit, bark, vermiculite, perlite or clay granules, and blends of 20-30% compost are common for transplanting seedlings. Seeding directly into compost is not advised: it dries fast, immature compost may hold germination-inhibiting phytotoxins, and undecomposed lignin may tie up nitrogen. Ready compost is dark brown or black with an earthy smell, and it can increase plant immunity to diseases and pests. Finished compost supplies little readily available nitrogen, since composting converts much N to stable organic forms while P and K availability is unchanged. It still releases other nutrients slowly and raises organic matter. Annual high rates set by nitrogen need overload soil with phosphorus and potassium, and salts may build up under high tunnels and greenhouses. Soil tests should guide a switch to {{ref:soil-agri-181}}.

soil-fert-147.title: Nitrobacter, living on a thin energy margin
soil-fert-147.text: Nitrobacter lives on scraps. Oxidizing nitrite to nitrate yields only −74 kJ per mole of nitrite, so its metabolism is highly specialized. This genus of rod-shaped, gram-negative bacteria performs the second step of {{ref:soil-fert-112}} in soil and the sea, and it fixes carbon dioxide through the {{ref:soil-hist-149}}. All members are obligate aerobes with a doubling time of about 13 hours, so oxygen and phosphorus tend to limit them. Widespread in water and soil, it makes nitrate, a primary source of inorganic nitrogen for plants. It grows best at pH 7.3 to 7.5. Winogradsky named the genus in 1892.

soil-fert-187.title: Soil tests: asking a field what it lacks
soil-fert-187.text: Before adding fertilizer, a grower can ask the soil what it needs. A soil test is a laboratory or in-situ analysis of a soil's chemical, physical or biological characteristics. The most widely run tests estimate plant-available nutrient concentrations to guide fertilizer recommendations. It reveals deficiencies and possible toxicities, and it is meant to mimic how roots take up minerals. Sampling matters. Labs such as Iowa State and Colorado State recommend 10–20 sample points per 40 acres, and composite sampling mixes soil from several spots. Nutrients vary with depth and time, so samples are best analyzed within about 24 hours, or else frozen or air-dried. Methods differ widely. Europe alone uses more than 10 tests for plant-available phosphorus, and their results are not directly comparable. Some labs analyze all 13 {{ref:soil-fert-289}} plus a dozen potentially toxic elements with one 'universal soil extractant', ammonium bicarbonate DTPA. Do-it-yourself kits usually test only N, P, K and pH and are less accurate.

soil-fert-263.title: Nitrogen and phosphorus: two nutrients, opposite habits
soil-fert-263.text: Nitrogen moves; phosphorus mostly stays put. That contrast shapes how each is supplied, lost and managed. Nitrogen comes mainly from decomposing organic matter and can be added biologically by legumes ({{ref:soil-fert-099}}, {{ref:soil-fert-127}}). No biological process adds phosphorus, which also comes from soil minerals. Nitrate, the main form plants absorb, is very mobile. Phosphorus movement is very limited, and its available form is a small dissolved amount, mainly H2PO4- and HPO4 2-. Most N loss is {{ref:soil-agri-022}}, denitrification or ammonia volatilization. Leaching dominates in sandy soils and denitrification in heavy loams and clays. Phosphorus is lost mainly in runoff and eroded sediment, but low losses have a high effect per unit on water quality because P often limits freshwater algae. P leaching matters in artificially drained fields: after years of excess manure or compost, P-saturated sandy soils leak P, and {{ref:soil-fert-211}} can flow through wormholes and cracks to drain lines. Cover crops store nitrogen that would otherwise leach, and mobilize P through mycorrhizae and store it for the next crop. Excess N pollutes water with nitrate, raises nitrous oxide from denitrification, wastes energy in manufacture, speeds loss of soil organic matter and is linked to more insect damage. Making, hauling and applying N fertilizer ({{ref:soil-fert-007}}) is about 30 percent of the energy used to grow corn.

soil-fert-270.title: Managing nitrogen and phosphorus: count, test, time, place, cover
soil-fert-270.text: Nitrogen and phosphorus behave differently in soil ({{ref:soil-fert-263}}), yet they need similar management. Take all nutrient sources into account, using soil, manure and compost tests, crop residue N, and the 4R principles of right rate, time, place and source, plus conservation practices. Place fertilizer below the surface, split N applications where leaching or denitrification threaten, and apply when leaching and runoff threats are minimal. Cover crops with minimal or no tillage improve structure, cut leaching, runoff and denitrification, and store N and P in organic form between cash crops. {{ref:soil-agri-098}} also keeps mycorrhizal networks intact for P. Sod-type forage crops in rotation reduce {{ref:soil-agri-022}} and P runoff, and {{ref:soil-agri-182}} such as cereal rye capture leftover nitrate. Time N close to crop uptake. Holding most fertilizer until a PSNT, sensor or model shows need lets sidedress N be applied only if wanted.

soil-bio-040.title: The earthworm, which Darwin ranked among history's great movers
soil-bio-040.text: In 1881 Charles Darwin wrote that few other animals had played so important a part in the history of the world. He meant the earthworm, a soil-dwelling invertebrate of the phylum Annelida. The name covers the largest members of the Oligochaeta. Earthworms live mostly in moist, compost-rich soil. They eat the remains of dead plants and animals, along with {{ref:soil-bio-274}}, {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, bacteria, fungi and algae, and rank among nature's most important eaters of dead matter. Adults range from 10 mm to 3 m long, though the typical common earthworm grows to about 360 mm. A worm moves by waves of muscle contraction, anchored by bristles called setae. It has no special respiratory organs and breathes through its moist skin. Populations depend on soil temperature, moisture, pH, salts, aeration and texture. Most favor neutral to slightly acidic soils, and their activity can shift pH to suit them. As they feed and burrow they aerate and mix the soil, help release nutrients for plants to take up, and bind soil organic matter to soil minerals. That makes them indicators of soil health. Healthy soil holds more of them, and their gut microbes reveal its condition. They are also vulnerable. {{ref:soil-fert-007}} create acidity fatal to worms, and pesticides kill them. At least three species are listed as extinct and many more as endangered.

soil-bio-025.title: The soil food web, a digestive system for the land
soil-bio-025.text: All soil organic matter passes through a living gut of sorts. The soil food web is the community of organisms living all or part of their lives in soil. It is seen as a network of feeding links that passes energy among them. A food chain follows one linear energy pathway; a food web shows all the potential pathways. Plants are the producers. Using sunlight, they make plant material from carbon dioxide and minerals, and their roots exude acids, sugars and enzymes that feed the web underground. Its members range from bacteria, algae, fungi and single-celled animals to {{ref:soil-bio-193}} and {{ref:soil-bio-209}}, and on to earthworms, insects and small vertebrates. Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break dead plant and animal material into simple nutrients. In this way the web processes dead material much as a digestive system processes food. The work reaches beyond the soil. The web keeps manure, plant residues and pesticides out of water, holds nitrogen back from groundwater, fixes nitrogen and helps water soak in. Its members prey on crop pests and feed animals above ground. Once thought simple, soil food webs turned out to have common omnivory and long, complex chains. Those chains still resist drying, freezing and fumigation. Some influence escapes the diagram, though. Litter transformers, mutualists and {{ref:soil-bio-004}} strongly affect their communities in ways food webs do not capture.

soil-chem-071.title: Living chelators: how microbes and roots fetch metals
soil-chem-071.text: Living things make their own claws for metal. Natural chelating agents are molecules made by organisms that bind metal ions as chelates: proteins, long-chain sugars, organic acids and microbial pigments. Malate, glutamic acid, histidine and the peptide phytochelatin are typical. Pseudomonas bacteria secrete the water-soluble pigments pyochelin and pyoverdine, which bind iron, and some root-dwelling bacteria use such pigments to hand iron to plants. Organic chelators such as peptides and sugars are even credited with chemical weathering, pulling metal ions out of rocks.

soil-form-164.title: Prairie dark soils and the grasses that made them
soil-form-164.text: Across the Prairies, the great groups of the {{ref:soil-class-123}} order follow the native grasses, which follow the regional water deficit. They are separated by the color of the A horizon, which shows how much organic carbon the grasses added. In the driest part, with an annual water deficit near 200 mm, low grasses with little biomass give Brown soils of that order; less deficit to the west and north gives Dark Brown and Black ones. Organic carbon is highest in southern Manitoba, where the deficit is only about 70 mm. All have organically enriched Ah horizons over decalcified, slightly reddened Bm horizons.

soil-bio-253.title: Exoenzymes: digesting food before eating it
soil-bio-253.text: A bacterium cannot swallow a log, so it digests the log from outside. Exoenzymes are enzymes a cell secretes to work beyond its walls, most often breaking large molecules apart. The small pieces can pass through the cell membrane and be used inside. There, endoenzymes, which work within the cell, finish the processing. Bacteria and fungi feed this way. In soil, cellulases target carbohydrates, oxidases lignin, phosphate-releasing enzymes organic phosphates, chitinases chains of {{ref:soil-bio-260}} and proteases proteins. Grouped as hydrolases, lyases, oxidoreductases and transferases, they set the pace of {{ref:soil-bio-039}} activity by degrading biopolymers. Fungi used to clean polluted ground secrete oxidative exoenzymes, such as laccases, from their growing hyphal tips. Cell-free exoenzymes can also clean up pollution, but they are often fragile and hard to get into soil. The word entered English in 1908; pepsin and trypsin were probably the first known.

soil-water-073.title: The ion cloud that decides whether clay holds together
soil-water-073.text: Salt can decide whether a clay stands firm. Clay platelets carry permanent and pH-dependent negative charges, as {{ref:soil-chem-079}} describes, balanced by cations such as Na+ on their surfaces, in interlayers or in the pore water. The electrical double layer is that cloud of balancing cations around each platelet, and its thickness depends on the water's salinity. In salty water the layer is compressed, so the platelets flocculate into stable aggregates. When rain leaches salt out of uplifted clay laid down in the sea, the layer expands. Stronger repulsion then disperses the platelets, called peptization, and the clay is destabilized. Adding salt back compresses the layer again, and {{ref:soil-water-071}} rapidly regains its strength.

soil-fert-274.title: Managing soils overloaded with phosphorus
soil-fert-274.text: A survey found the average US dairy herd was fed about 25 percent more P than the National Research Council recommends. High-P soils result from excessive P fertilizer or, more often, heavy manure use ({{ref:soil-fert-254}}), and they need managing to limit phosphorus loss to water. They are common on livestock farms with limited land and imported feed, where feed nutrients exceed those exported in animal products and where manure or compost applied to meet N adds extra P. The extra supplemental P can cost thousands of dollars for a 100-cow herd and ends up as a potential pollutant. Risk depends on context. Sites near critical water with slope, fine texture, poor structure or poor drainage need aggressive measures, while flat, grass-bordered vegetable or urban plots pose far less. First cut P in animal diets, then stop extra P by spreading manure on more land, swapping fields, or using legume covers and forages for N. Do not use a high-P source such as compost to supply N, since P builds up over the long term. Reduce runoff and erosion with {{ref:soil-agri-098}}, contour strips, cover crops, {{ref:soil-water-109}} and buffers. Tile drainage can still carry P, especially after heavy liquid manure. Soil-test P falls slowly once imports stop, so test every two to three years. A one-time tillage can redistribute P built up at the surface of no-till soil, followed by starter P and injected manure.

soil-bio-318.title: The Walkley-Black method and its biases
soil-bio-318.text: The Walkley-Black method oxidizes organic carbon with chromate, heated by added sulfuric acid, and titrates the leftover chromate to get the carbon. It was once the standard method. It oxidizes carbon incompletely, so a correction factor that varies with soil type is needed, and this biases the results. Carbon present as charcoal may be missed, which underestimates total carbon in the soil.

soil-hist-147.title: Photosynthesis: how light becomes the food that feeds soil
soil-hist-147.text: Every sugar in a plant, and so nearly every scrap of organic matter in soil, began as light. Photosynthesis is the biological process by which plants, algae and cyanobacteria convert light energy into chemical energy stored in organic compounds. Usually the term means oxygenic photosynthesis, which splits water and releases oxygen. The stored carbohydrates are later used in cellular respiration, a reaction type that {{ref:soil-chem-113}} describes. In plants, chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs red and blue light. The light reactions make NADPH and ATP, and the {{ref:soil-hist-149}} then builds sugars from atmospheric CO2. The scale is planetary. Photosynthesis maintains atmospheric oxygen and supplies most biological energy. Globally it captures about 130 terawatts and fixes 100-115 billion tons of carbon into biomass yearly. Individual plants are less impressive. They convert light with an efficiency usually of 3-6%, ranging from 0.1% to 8% with light, temperature and CO2. The process was long misunderstood. In 1779 Jan Ingenhousz showed that plants need light, not just soil and water.

soil-class-149.title: Plaggen soils, built one sod at a time
soil-class-149.text: Farmers in north-west Europe built their own soil, one sod at a time, from the Middle Ages on. They cut sods of shrubland or grass with roots and humus, and used them as bedding for cattle or sheep. In spring they spread the slurry-soaked bedding on their fields as manure. Centuries of this turned poor Podzols into plaggen soil, a deep, humus-rich plaggic Anthrosol 40 cm to over 1.50 m deep. Modern arable soils reach about 30 cm. The fields rose with sharp edges, called Plaggenesche in Germany or Es in Dutch. The practice ended around 1900 with the arrival of fertilizers. Orkney had such soils by the 12th to 13th centuries, and parts of Shetland kept the method until the 1960s. Far away, Maori farmers in New Zealand used plaggen-like practices to improve drainage for kumara.

soil-form-140.title: Primary minerals, inherited unchanged from rock
soil-form-140.text: Much of a soil's grit was never made in the soil at all. Soil minerals come in two types. Primary minerals are found in soil but did not form there. They crystallized with their host igneous rock and have not been chemically altered since. {{ref:soil-chem-235}}, by contrast, form as primary minerals weather. Primary mineral particles are mostly larger than 2 μm. They make up the silt, sand and gravel fractions. {{ref:soil-form-135}} supplies them: quartz, {{ref:soil-form-141}}, {{ref:soil-form-142}}, {{ref:soil-chem-226}}, {{ref:soil-form-144}}, amphibole, pyroxene and {{ref:soil-form-145}}. Silicates dominate the primary minerals in soil, and quartz and cristobalite are common soil tectosilicates, silicates built as a three-dimensional framework. The chain runs from primary rocks, the source of primary minerals, to the parent rocks those minerals compose.

soil-bio-014.title: The soil's single-celled grazers
soil-bio-014.text: Heterotrophic flagellates may occasionally number several million in a gram of soil. They are the smallest of these grazers, single-celled eukaryotes grouped as flagellates, amoebae and ciliates. Most of them eat bacteria. Others eat bacteria and fungi, fungi alone, or particles of decayed plant and animal matter. Naked amoebae move through water-filled pores and films. {{ref:soil-bio-195}} shelter in shells against drying out, and they serve as indicators of past climates. Ciliates, the largest, move by many short beating cilia.

soil-bio-011.title: Soil microbiology and the 33,000 species on a beet root
soil-bio-011.text: In 2011, researchers detected more than 33,000 bacterial and archaeal species on the roots of sugar beet. Soil microbiology studies such microorganisms: what they do and how they affect soil properties. Its subjects are grouped as bacteria, including cyanobacteria and actinomycetes, archaea, fungi, algae, slime molds and {{ref:soil-bio-274}}. Their history is long. The first cyanobacteria arose two to four billion years ago. They fixed carbon and nitrogen, releasing oxygen into the air and nitrogen into the soil. How diverse a soil's microbes are depends on its pH, texture, soil organic matter content, plant community and contaminants such as heavy metals. That diversity pays off. Microbes make soil nutrients more available to plants, produce growth hormones, stimulate plant immunity and trigger or dampen plant stress responses. A more diverse soil microbiome, the whole community of soil microbes, generally brings fewer plant diseases and higher crop yields. The microbes also signal to one another through soluble metabolites, volatile organic compounds and extracellular sugar polymers. They trade metabolites that support each other's growth. Farmers can encourage them: sowing {{ref:soil-agri-066}} raises microbial activity, improving nitrogen availability, crop nitrogen uptake and yields.

soil-hist-034.title: Rethinking what soil organic matter is
soil-hist-034.text: Historically, stability was blamed on humic substances, formed from inputs and extracted with strong base and acid, then interpreted as large stable macromolecules. From the late 1990s high-resolution chemistry showed that {{ref:soil-found-045}} is recognizable plant and animal biomolecules at varying degradation stages, which can associate like larger molecules. Flaws in the old view showed in 1999, when soil models could not account for the large charcoal component of {{ref:soil-class-123}} soils. A newer paradigm holds that molecular structure alone does not explain persistence. Microbial carbon-use efficiency matters, and labile molecules taken up by microbes may form most stable organic matter. The debate is live. The {{ref:soil-chem-063}} still appears in textbooks while some researchers argue it is wrong. Compare {{ref:soil-bio-090}} and the {{ref:soil-bio-092}}.

soil-bio-256.title: The acid enzyme that unlocks bound phosphorus
soil-bio-256.text: Much soil phosphorus is bound inside organic molecules, out of reach. An acid-working enzyme frees it. This enzyme strips attached phosphate groups from other molecules, working best at an acidic {{ref:soil-found-014}} below 7. It uses water to split a phosphate monoester into an alcohol and phosphate. Soil microorganisms rely on it to reach organically bound phosphate. Some roots, especially cluster roots, exude carboxylates with this activity to mobilize phosphorus in poor soils. Measuring its activity reveals how much a soil's life is demanding phosphate.

soil-fert-292.title: Fertilizer or organic source: choosing what to apply
soil-fert-292.text: Commercial fertilizers such as {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, triple {{ref:soil-fert-094}} and muriate of potash are convenient, easy to blend, predictable and precise in timing and rate. They have drawbacks. Common nitrogen materials are acid forming, nitrogen fertilizer takes 25%-50% of the energy in growing corn, and high solubility can cause salt or ammonia damage to seedlings and greater losses if mismanaged. Slow-release forms, such as sulfur- or polymer-coated granules, and {{ref:soil-fert-013}}, better match supply to crop needs. Organic sources are the nutrients in crop residues, manures and composts. Organic farmers replace synthetic fertilizers with minerals like greensand, granite dust and rock phosphate, or with bone, fish, soybean and blood meal. The cheapest source is not always best: anhydrous ammonia is hard to inject in stony soil, {{ref:soil-fert-206}} gives 18% N with phosphorus, and potassium magnesium sulfate suits fields needing magnesium but no lime.

soil-fert-257.title: Dung patches: uneven fertility on pasture
soil-fert-257.text: A grazing animal fertilizes in spots. Animals on pasture drop excrement on the surface, making small concentrated nutrient spots between which the soil is poorer. Some ammonium and urea is lost to the air as the pies dry. Dense vegetation keeps runoff low and nitrogen leaching less of a concern. Yet because the patches are unevenly spread, nitrate can still leach on intensively managed, fertilized dairy pasture.

soil-fert-124.title: Nitrogen deposition: fertilizer falling from the sky
soil-fert-124.text: Reactive nitrogen falls from the sky. Nitrogen deposition is its arrival from the atmosphere onto land and water. It comes as nitrate, ammonium and organic nitrogen in rain and snow, as ammonia and nitric acid gases, or as fine aerosol particles of the salt in {{ref:soil-fert-071}}. More of it can acidify soils, streams and lakes and change forest and grassland productivity. Grasslands gain at first, then decline past critical thresholds. Extra nitrogen favours fast-growing plants that shade out slower ones, so species richness falls. On nitrogen-poor shrubland, invading grasses replace the native dwarf shrubs. Ammonia and ammonium can also harm plants adapted to nitrate, stunting their roots and shoots.

soil-bio-002.title: Billions in a teaspoon: the bacteria of the soil
soil-bio-002.text: A teaspoon of productive soil holds 100 million to 3 billion bacteria. In and around plant roots, up to 10 billion culturable cells live in each gram. Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes, cells without a nucleus, and they are the soil's most numerous inhabitants. They live in soil water, including the moisture film around particles, where some swim with whip-like flagella. When conditions suit, they multiply fast by splitting in two. Most beneficial soil bacteria need oxygen and are most active in moist but unsaturated soil of neutral pH with plenty of food. Those that live without oxygen tend to putrefy dead plant and animal matter. Away from roots, most rest as drought-resistant colonies in a sugar-polymer matrix coated with clay platelets. They wait until {{ref:soil-bio-142}} or earthworm mucus reach them. Hostile conditions send them dormant: Gram-positive Bacillus and Clostridium form spores, and Gram-negative bacteria enter a resting stage in which they cannot be cultured. Bacteria run key steps of the {{ref:soil-fert-099}}. Some capture nitrogen from the air, some turn ammonia toward nitrate, and others return nitrate to gas where oxygen is absent. Pseudomonas can metabolize a wide range of chemicals, while {{ref:soil-fert-147}} gets its energy only by oxidizing nitrite to nitrate. Soil archaea, also prokaryotes, are still poorly known but may matter in that ammonia-to-nitrate step and in methanogenesis. Some bacteria colonize minerals and speed their weathering.

soil-fert-232.title: Phosphorus deficiency and the purple warning
soil-fert-232.text: Most of the phosphorus in a soil sits in forms plants cannot absorb. Plants take it up as phosphate ions, and soil pH sets which forms of phosphate exist; between pH 6 and 7 the least is bound up. Phosphorus deficiency slows maturity and makes plants store excess starch. Some turn dark purple from anthocyanin, a pigment, but only once the shortage is fairly severe. Soil tests such as Bray 1-P, Mehlich 3 and Olsen extract phosphorus for colorimetric measurement. Roots fight back by favoring lateral roots and secreting phosphate-releasing enzymes and organic acids. Larger roots and mycorrhizal partners raise uptake.

soil-fert-249.title: How much manure to spread
soil-fert-249.text: Farmers usually spread manure at a rate judged to supply the current crop's nitrogen, drawing on the forms described in {{ref:soil-fert-246}}. Common dairy rates are 10-30 tons solid or 4,000-11,000 gallons liquid per acre, supplying about 50-150 pounds available N. Small grains need 10-15 tons, corn 20-30 tons. Higher rates may build organic matter but risk nitrate buildup in leafy crops, {{ref:soil-agri-022}}, salt damage and excess soil phosphorus. Where soil P is far above optimum, apply by crop P need and export part of the manure. Manure on legumes is discouraged, because the legume then fixes less N, though it can suit intensive animal farms with excess N. Manure P and K availability resembles fertilizer. Twenty tons of dairy manure give about 30-50 pounds phosphate and 180-200 pounds potash.

soil-hist-012.title: Peter Erasmus Müller reads the forest floor
soil-hist-012.text: Peter Erasmus Müller (1840–1926), a Danish forester and naturalist, described mor humus for the first time. He called it beech peat, by analogy with sphagnum peat. His Studies on Forest Soil ran as a series in 1878–84 in a journal he had founded in 1875, the first independent Danish forestry journal. It was translated into German and French. The studies showed how plant communities and their animals shape the ground surface, as in moorland formation. His last major work, in 1924, concluded that the Danish moors continue the tundra that arose after the ice age and were never forested like nearby land.

soil-bio-050.title: Biofilms, the slime cities where soil bacteria live
soil-bio-050.text: In soil and on plant surfaces, most bacteria live bound in biofilms, nicknamed cities for microbes. A biofilm is a community of microorganisms whose cells stick to each other, and often to a surface, inside a self-made slime described in {{ref:soil-bio-080}}. The slime mixes long sugar chains, proteins, lipids and DNA, and can hold many times its dry weight in water. It shelters residents, lets them share nutrients and keeps enzymes close as an external digestion system. Soils with more clay minerals hold more bacteria as biofilms on clay surfaces. On roots, biofilms of growth-promoting bacteria such as Bacillus, Pseudomonas and the genus in {{ref:soil-bio-237}} can prime a plant's resistance to pathogens. Biofilms help cycle nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon and oxygen. Their internal gradients let nitrate-making microbes work near the surface, while oxygen-free microbes deeper inside run {{ref:soil-fert-108}}. In soil, biofilms can clog pores. In sewage works and slow sand filters they are put to work stripping pollutants from water.

soil-bio-080.title: Extracellular polymeric substances, the glue of microbial life
soil-bio-080.text: Between 50% and 90% of the organic material in a biofilm is the slime its microbes secrete. Extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) are high-molecular-weight natural polymers that microorganisms release into their surroundings. They are mostly long sugar chains and proteins, with DNA, lipids and humic compounds. They hold biofilms together and protect the microbes inside from harsh conditions, mechanical removal and antimicrobials. Sugar-polymer slimes help nitrogen-fixing bacteria attach to plant roots and soil particles, so the bacteria can colonize roots and the soil around them. EPS also shape the soil itself. Together with microbial cells they can block soil pores in bioclogging, lowering hydraulic conductivity. They make sediment more stable by changing its cohesion, permeability and erosion, and they affect the precipitation of minerals, especially carbonates. They adsorb metal cations such as copper, lead, nickel and cadmium, which helps clean up heavy metals. EPS from the bacterium Zoogloea and the fungus Aspergillus niger even remove {{ref:soil-env-199}} from contaminated soils, using enzymes that degrade them.

soil-bio-141.title: Root mucilage, the slime that greases every root tip
soil-bio-141.text: Plants use up to 40% of the energy they make by photosynthesis secreting one product: slime. Root mucilage is a gelatinous secretion of plant-specific long chains of sugars, that coats the protective tip described in {{ref:soil-bio-198}} as part of the root exudate. How it is secreted is still debated. Growing evidence points to root-cap cells that are continually shed and burst as roots push through soil, releasing sugar chains made in their Golgi apparatus and cell walls. Maize mucilage is rich in galactose, xylose, arabinose, rhamnose and glucose, the building blocks of pectin and other plant sugar polymers. Mucilage glues soil to the root, keeping the contact needed to regulate water uptake. It cuts friction as roots penetrate and maintains a microclimate. It can also reduce evaporation and store water, which helps plants cope with water deficit. Soil fungi feed on broken-down mucilage and in return raise the plant's uptake of water and nutrients, particularly phosphorus.

soil-bio-118.title: Particulate organic matter, the fast fuel of soil life
soil-bio-118.text: Pass soil through a fine sieve, and some organic matter stays behind. Particulate organic matter, or POM, is the fraction that does not pass a filter or sieve with openings usually between 0.053 millimeters (53 μm) and 2 millimeters. It still shows its original cellular structure: partly decomposed plant litter, animal feces, microbial detritus and pollen. Its carbon is particulate organic carbon, or POC, and there is typically about twice as much POM as POC. Most POM turns over in less than 10 years, though less active parts may take 15 to 100 years. Its decay supplies much of the energy of soil organisms and a steady release of nutrients. Fungal threads colonizing it bind particles with sticky sugar polymers into aggregates, improving infiltration, aeration and resistance to erosion. Manure and crop residues raise POM, while repeated working of the soil and turning native grassland into farmland deplete it. Because it responds quickly to management, it is often used as an indicator of soil quality.

soil-bio-090.title: Humification, how part of the litter becomes humus
soil-bio-090.text: Not all decaying matter vanishes into carbon dioxide. In humification, soil organisms feeding on litter turn part of it into humus instead of mineralizing it completely. The raw materials are plant detritus, dead animals and microbes, called necromass, the excreta of all soil organisms and black carbon from past fires. Fungi and bacteria that feed on dead matter do the work, along with earthworms, nematodes, protozoa and arthropods. Earthworms are major contributors. The ingredients disappear in order. Sugars, starches, simple proteins and organic acids go first and fast. Cellulose and {{ref:soil-bio-116}} follow more slowly, and fats, waxes and resins persist longest. {{ref:soil-bio-129}} transform that tough polymer quickly, making it a main precursor of humus. Resistant leftovers, such as modified {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, oils, fats and waxes, join newly made compounds like long sugar chains to form the basis of humus. Reactions with proteins lock nitrogen and other nutrients inside, protecting them from mineralization. Early work pictured humification as building polymers that microbes could not attack. Recent research shows microbes can digest humic substances in redox reactions. Humification happens naturally in soil and artificially in {{ref:soil-fert-029}}, and it can darken soils, a change called melanization. For storing carbon long term, stimulating it beats slowing litter decay. Not everyone accepts the idea, though. Some authors reject humification as a distinct process, arguing that soil organic matter is a continuum of progressively decomposing compounds.

soil-fert-130.title: Enzymes that free phosphorus from dead matter
soil-fert-130.text: Plant growth depends on roots quickly taking up the phosphorus released from dead organic matter. Organic phosphorus mineralization is the breakdown of organic phosphorus compounds by enzymes into free phosphate that plants and microbes can use. Phosphate-releasing enzymes, nucleases and phytase are among the enzymes involved, members of the group in {{ref:soil-bio-039}}. This hydrolysis, the splitting of molecules with water, is essential for plant and microbial nutrition, and it moves organic phosphorus from soil to water. The activity of these enzymes in soil can serve as an indicator of phosphorus mineralization potential and availability.

soil-form-164.q: What separates the great groups of the order of dark prairie soils?
soil-form-164.a: The colour of the A horizon, which shows how much organic carbon the grasses added.

soil-bio-256.q: What reaction does the acid enzyme that unlocks bound phosphorus catalyse, and at what pH does it work best?
soil-bio-256.a: It hydrolyses a phosphate monoester with water to give an alcohol and phosphate, at an optimum pH below 7.

soil-fert-130.q: What can the activity of phosphate-releasing enzymes in soil indicate?
soil-fert-130.a: The soil's potential for phosphorus mineralization and its phosphorus availability.
